To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
type A CBM3acips specifically bind to xyloglucoan in solution and that the nature of the interaction is driven by enthalpy.

the CBM3ac from the CipA cellulose binding protein from Clostridium thermocellum binds to xyloglucose in solution and on surfaces and that the nature of this binding is different from that of cellulose.
type A CBM3acips can bind to XG, that XG binds in the same site as cellulose and that binding to XG is enthalpic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of CBM‐cellulose interactions.
the recognition of xyloglucas by type A CBMs.
the molecular basis of polysaccharide binding to CBMs and the role of CBM‐ligand interactions in cell wall architecture and function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
type A CBM3s bind to crystalline cellulose, but can also bind to other β‐1, 4‐glucans such as xyloglucans.
type A CBM‐polymers can bind through enthalpic interactions, but the enthalpic interactions are driven by a range of factors including the hydrophobicity and the presence of aromatic residues.
the type A CBMs are able to bind to both crystalline cellulose and to xyloglucas.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the binding of type A CBM3 to xyloglucas is driven by enthalpy, and the binding is not entropically driven.
CBMs can be used as tools for studying the structure of cell walls, and that CBMs can recognize a variety of polysaccharides.
type A CBM3s bind to both xyloglucans and celluloses with comparable affinity and that the binding is driven by enthalpy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CBMs can bind to both crystalline and amorphous polysaccharides, and that this binding can be enthalpic.
type A non‐catabolic CBMs can bind to XG.
the binding of type A CBM3a to cellulose and xyloglucans is driven by enthalpy, and that these interactions are not driven by entropic effects.
